title: Yogācāra’s Storehouse Consciousness — continuity without a permanent self
when: The store-consciousness idea developed in layered early Yogācāra literature, whose texts are difficult to date precisely. Asaṅga and Vasubandhu systematized the tradition around the fourth–fifth centuries CE.
people: Asaṅga and Vasubandhu; authors of the Yogācārabhūmi and related Mahāyāna texts.
origin: Indian Mahāyāna Buddhism, in intellectual and meditative communities debating karma, rebirth, and the Buddhist teaching of not-self.
idea: In classical Yogācāra, ālayavijñāna (“storehouse” or “substratum consciousness”) is a subtle, changing stream that supports other forms of consciousness. Intentional actions and experiences leave “seeds”—dispositions that may later mature into perceptions, habits, and karmic results. This helps explain continuity through sleep, deep meditation, and rebirth without positing an unchanging soul. The store consciousness is not a hidden permanent self: it is conditioned, and its role is transformed or brought to an end in awakening. Yogācāra texts assign it several related functions, and scholars debate how the theory first developed.
relevance: The theory offers a historically specific account of how learned dispositions shape experience without a fixed inner owner. It invites comparison with modern theories of habit and unconscious processing, but ālayavijñāna is not simply an ancient version of the modern unconscious.

sources.name: Mind in Indian Buddhist Philosophy, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
